tagline.text: A 1914 house museum in the heart of Quiapo, home to Katipunan heroes

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱80–300 (admission, transport and snacks, per person)

children.text: Bahay Nakpil-Bautista is a two-storey bahay na bato house built in Quiapo in 1914, now a museum that was once home to Katipunan revolutionary Julio Nakpil and Gregoria de Jesus. It is within walking distance of Quiapo Church and mainly opens on Saturdays.

Bahay Nakpil-Bautista is a two-storey house at 432 A. Bautista Street (formerly Barbosa Street) in the Quiapo district of Manila. The architect Arcadio Arellano built it in 1914 for the physician Dr. Ariston Bautista and his wife, the painter Petrona Nakpil, and it is said to have originally stood on two lots totaling about 500 square meters. Today it serves as a museum and cultural space managed by the Nakpil family and the Bahay Nakpil-Bautista Foundation.

What makes this house special is its people. Julio Nakpil was a general of the Philippine Revolution and a composer. Gregoria de Jesus, the widow of Andrés Bonifacio, later married Julio Nakpil. Juan Nakpil became the first National Artist for architecture, and Francisco Nakpil was a silversmith and member of La Liga Filipina. Each of them occupies a chapter of modern Philippine history, which is why the house carries the nickname "Tahanan ng mga Katipunero" (Home of the Katipuneros).

The architecture is worth a look too. A stone ground floor carries a wooden upper floor in the traditional bahay na bato manner, blended with the Vienna Secession style that was fashionable in the early 20th century. The highlights are the window grilles with floral and lyre motifs, furniture designed to match those motifs, and the calados, openings cut into the walls to let air flow through. The wooden upper floor is said to have been built to withstand earthquakes.

The National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) declared the house a cultural property on August 25, 2011, and it is also classed as a National Historical Landmark. Close to Quiapo Church, it makes a calm, non-air-conditioned hour in the middle of a hectic Quiapo day. Opening days are very limited, so always check the official announcement before you go. A visit takes one to two hours at most, longer if you join a guided talk or linger over photos. This is not a large museum; the point is walking through a house where people really lived, so go to enjoy the atmosphere of the rooms and their stories rather than expecting grand exhibits.

blocks.title: A house in Vienna Secession style

children.text: Window grilles with floral and lyre motifs, furniture matched to those motifs and breezy calado walls all come together in one house. This early 20th-century European-influenced design is rare among traditional Philippine houses. The ground floor has the zaguan where carriages were parked, a bedroom, a living room and a patio, while the upper floor has an anteroom, living room, dining room, azotea and kitchen, so you can picture how a well-off family of the period moved through the house.

blocks.title: The Katipunan revolution and this house

children.text: Julio Nakpil was a general of the revolution, and several members of the family took part in the revolutionary and reform movements. Understanding why the house is called a site of modern Philippine history is the starting point for your visit. Ask whether a guided explanation is available.

blocks.title: Bahay ni Giliw and the women of the house

children.text: The official website presents a section called "Ang mga Maybahay" (the mistresses of the house) along with curator's notes. It tells the stories of women of the revolutionary era, including Gregoria de Jesus, who was married to Bonifacio and later to Julio Nakpil, through the setting of a home. The detailed exhibit layout may change between visits.
This space honors Julio Nakpil, revolutionary general and composer. The official website also presents his musical works and visual art interpretations as a virtual exhibit.

The official website introduces the house as the "Home of the Katipuneros" and has a separate section on the 1896–1898 Revolution. It lets you view the revolution from the perspective of the home rather than the battlefield.

blocks.title: The upper-floor museum and its objects

children.text: The upper floor serves as a museum honoring the Nakpil family, Julio Nakpil and Gregoria de Jesus, with Katipunan-related items and paintings. Old documents, letters and books, vintage furniture and a piano also catch the eye.

According to May 2026 reports by Vogue Philippines and Kanto, the exterior was recently repainted green. Scraping back the layers of paint revealed shades of light green, which guided the choice, though the original shade could not be determined exactly.

blocks.title: A refuge for the Black Nazarene

children.text: The house is said to have sheltered a Black Nazarene statue from Quiapo Church during the bombings of World War II. Wikipedia calls it the original image, while a travel blog says it was a replica, so accounts differ. It is a good anecdote to share alongside a Quiapo pilgrimage.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: Quiapo Church and the house museum

children.text: Start at
Quiapo Church
. Look around the church and the plaza in front, and enjoy the street stalls outside. Many devotees come to venerate the Black Nazarene, so keep an eye on your belongings.
Walk to A. Bautista Street to match the opening hours. Saturday opening is the rule, so plan to arrive after
. Announce your visit at the entrance and buy your ticket.
See the carriage parking area (zaguan), living room and patio on the ground floor, then climb the stairs to the upper floor. Look at the calado walls and the grille patterns.
Take your time in the upper-floor museum with its Katipunan items, the Julio Nakpil Room and the paintings. Ask whether a guided explanation is available.
Browse books and postcards at the gift shop, then grab a snack or lunch near the Quiapo market.

Opening hours are short, so aim to enter before 11:00. Calling or emailing just before your visit to confirm it is open can save you a wasted trip. The house has narrow stairs and corridors, and movement slows when it gets crowded. Groups should contact the museum beforehand to arrange an entry time.
Start with about
1 hour
at the house museum, hearing the stories of the revolutionary era.
Stroll around Quiapo Church and the nearby market lanes. The exact route depends on local conditions.
Head to
Binondo Chinatown
for lunch. It is close by, but the trip can take time depending on traffic.
Continue to
Intramuros
to see the walls and churches.
The official website says the house can be reached by public transport from Quezon Boulevard and from the junction of C.M. Recto Street and F.R. Hidalgo Street.
The usual way is to take the Manila light rail (LRT) to a station near Quiapo, then walk toward Quiapo Church. Check station names and transfers on a map app before you go.
From the airport, the simplest option is a Grab or taxi to near Quiapo Church, then walk. Depending on traffic, the trip can take
40 minutes to 1.5 hours
or more.
Quiapo has heavy traffic and crowds, so leave with time to spare.
A. Bautista Street is one-way from F.R. Hidalgo Street and dead-ends at Escaldo Street.

Only a few cars or vans can park in front of the house, so if you drive, let the museum know of your arrival in advance. Buses cannot enter A. Bautista Street; per the official location page, paid parking is at a lot on Bilibid Viejo Street and free parking on nearby De Guzman and Hidalgo Streets.
If you use Grab, decide whether to set the pickup or drop-off as the house or Quiapo Church, and be aware that the one-way street may force a detour.
Comparing the coordinates on Wikipedia with those of Quiapo Church shows that the two sites are very close in a straight line.
Sidewalks and lanes are narrow and full of stalls, so walking is slow. Carry your backpack in front.
The official website states that the house has no air conditioning. On hot, humid days it can be hard to stay long, so the cooler dry season is much more comfortable.

Because the house mainly opens on Saturdays, the day of the week matters more than the season. It is closed on holidays and special holidays, so check the Philippine holiday calendar when planning. The area gets extremely crowded around the Black Nazarene festivities in early January, so check the latest announcements.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Comfortable for walking and good for photos. Expect crowds during Quiapo festival days.
With no air conditioning, go early in the morning. Bring water.
Bring an umbrella and a light jacket, and keep an eye on typhoon news.

The area around the house is a district of sights and markets rather than a place to stay, so it is better to book a hotel elsewhere, such as Intramuros, Ermita, Malate or Makati, and visit as a day trip. Quiapo is congested, so wandering around late in the evening is not recommended. After touring a house with no air conditioning you will want a cool drink and a place to rest, so a stop at a café near the church or toward the malls is a good idea.

You can eat at the street stalls and long-established eateries around Quiapo Church. Choose street food by checking hygiene with your own eyes. Heading to Binondo Chinatown opens up many more choices. Business hours change often, so confirm them locally.
According to the official website, the house is open only on Saturdays from
to
and closed on other days and on holidays. Earlier listings gave Tuesday to Sunday, and sources differ, so be sure to check before you set out.
Contact: mobile +63 917 871 7455, landline +63 2 8731 9305, email info@bahaynakpil.org. Some pages of the official site list the mobile as 917 851 7455, so email if the call does not connect.
If you bring a car, parking in front of the house is tight, so let them know you are coming.
There is no air conditioning, so bring light, breathable clothing, water and a small fan or handkerchief.
This is an old wooden building with many stairs. Non-slip shoes are best.
Pairing it with Quiapo Church as a morning outing makes getting around easy.
A little background reading on the Katipunan, Gregoria de Jesus and Julio Nakpil will make the exhibits much more meaningful.
Ask before you visit about rules for photography inside and for commercial shoots. Shoots may require extra fees and written reservations.

If you visit with a group or family, explaining to children that the Katipunan was the Philippines' secret society for independence is enough for them to follow along. The official page lists no separate children's rate, so ask.
Opening days are very limited. The official website says the house opens only on Saturdays, so a weekday visit may mean a wasted trip.

The official website notes that the house is old and has no accessibility facilities for persons with disabilities. A visitor write-up also mentions the stairs up from the ground floor to the mezzanine and a third floor open only to staff and volunteers for safety. Wheelchair users should ask in advance.
Quiapo is known for pickpockets and phone snatchers. Keep valuables in front of you.
The house is closed on holidays and special holidays. Check the calendar before you plan.
Admission fees and opening hours differ between sources and may have changed, so confirm with the official contacts before you visit.
The artifacts and furniture in the house are precious cultural property, so do not touch them.
The church known for the Black Nazarene is close enough to walk to. Many devotees gather there every Friday.
Often called the oldest Chinatown in the world. It is good for Chinese restaurants and markets, and a short ride from Quiapo.
The walled city of the Spanish colonial era. A good next stop for a full-day itinerary.
Stalls selling herbs, religious items and street food line the area around the church. It is fun to browse but crowded, so watch your belongings.
